fact: American bison are the largest land mammals in North America.
Moose are the largest members of the deer family.
Male elk grow large antlers that are shed and regrown each year.
White-tailed deer raise their white tails like flags when alarmed.
Mule deer have especially large ears that resemble a mule's ears.
Both male and female caribou can grow antlers.
Pronghorns are among the fastest land animals in North America.
Bighorn sheep have special hooves that help them grip steep rocky slopes.
Mountain goats are strong climbers with rough hoof pads for rocky terrain.
Musk oxen have extremely warm underfur called qiviut.
Grizzly bears have powerful shoulder muscles that help them dig.
American black bears can be black
Polar bears have black skin beneath their thick fur.
Gray wolves live and hunt in family groups called packs.
Coyotes communicate with howls
Red foxes use large ears to pinpoint small animals hidden under grass or snow.
Arctic foxes have fur-covered foot pads that help insulate them from cold ground.
Bobcats are named for their short bobbed tails.
Canada lynx have large furry paws that act like snowshoes.
Cougars can leap great distances and climb trees easily.
Wolverines have strong jaws and broad paws for traveling over snow.
American badgers have powerful forelimbs and long claws for digging.
Striped skunks can spray a strong-smelling liquid when threatened.
River otters are playful swimmers with webbed feet and streamlined bodies.
Sea otters use rocks as tools to open hard-shelled food.
Beavers build dams that can create ponds and wetlands.
Porcupines are covered with thousands of sharp quills made from modified hairs.
Raccoons have very sensitive front paws that help them explore objects and food.
Virginia opossums are North America's only native marsupials north of Mexico.
Nine-banded armadillos can jump straight upward when startled.
Cottontail rabbits are named for the fluffy white underside of their tails.
Snowshoe hares have large furry feet that help them move over snow.
Prairie dogs live in large burrow systems sometimes called towns.
Pikas collect grasses and flowers into hay piles for winter food.
Gray squirrels bury nuts and sometimes forget them
Red squirrels often store cones in piles called middens.
Groundhogs are large squirrels that dig deep burrows.
American martens are agile forest mammals that climb trees well.
Fishers are forest-dwelling relatives of weasels and are excellent climbers.
Ringtails have long striped tails and are nimble climbers of rocky cliffs and trees.
Bald eagles build some of the largest bird nests in North America.
Golden eagles use powerful talons to catch prey.
Great horned owls have feather tufts that look like ears.
Snowy owls have thick feathers that cover even their legs and feet.
Wild turkeys can fly short distances despite spending much of their time on the ground.
Sandhill cranes perform energetic dancing displays with jumps and bows.
Whooping cranes are among the tallest birds in North America.
American flamingos get their pink color from pigments in the food they eat.
Brown pelicans often plunge-dive from the air to catch fish.
Puffins use their wings to swim underwater.
Loons are excellent divers with legs set far back on their bodies.
Greater roadrunners can run quickly and often hunt lizards
Alligators use powerful tails to swim through water.
Gila monsters are venomous lizards with bead-like scales.
Desert tortoises spend much of their lives in underground burrows.
Snapping turtles have strong jaws and long tails.
American bullfrogs are large frogs with deep booming calls.
Hellbenders are giant salamanders that live in cool fast-moving streams.
Monarch butterflies can migrate thousands of miles between North America and Mexico.
American lobsters have large claws and live on the rocky seafloor of the North Atlantic.
